reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / KDIGO
clinicalPearls: Diabetic kidney disease is the leading cause of end-stage kidney disease worldwide and develops in a substantial proportion of people with long-standing type 1 or type 2 diabetes
The classic course progresses from glomerular hyperfiltration through rising albuminuria to declining glomerular filtration, though not every patient follows this sequence
Persistent albuminuria is both an early marker of kidney involvement and an independent predictor of cardiovascular risk
Coexisting diabetic retinopathy supports the diagnosis, and its absence in type 1 diabetes should prompt consideration of a non-diabetic cause
Features that argue against pure diabetic disease include an active urinary sediment, rapid loss of function, heavy proteinuria without retinopathy, or a short duration of diabetes
Control of blood pressure, glycaemia, and albuminuria, together with blockade of the renin-angiotensin system, are the mainstays of slowing progression
Newer agents that reduce intraglomerular pressure and albuminuria have been shown to slow decline and reduce cardiovascular events, changing modern management principles
Regular screening with albuminuria measurement and estimated GFR allows early intervention before irreversible damage accumulates
reference.pathophysiology: Diabetic kidney disease develops from chronic hyperglycaemia acting through several interlinked pathways. Excess glucose drives formation of advanced glycation end products, activation of protein kinase C, and oxidative stress, which damage the glomerular filtration barrier. Early on, altered afferent and efferent arteriolar tone produces glomerular hypertension and hyperfiltration, increasing shear stress on the capillary wall. Over time the glomerular basement membrane thickens, the mesangium expands with accumulation of matrix, and podocytes are lost, culminating in the nodular and diffuse glomerulosclerosis characteristic of the disease. These changes progressively increase albumin leakage and reduce filtration surface area. Systemic and intraglomerular hypertension, along with tubulointerstitial fibrosis, accelerates the decline toward end-stage kidney disease.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of chronic kidney disease coexisting with diabetes
additionalInvestigations: Quantification of albuminuria (urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio) and serial estimated GFR
Urinalysis with microscopy to detect an active sediment suggesting an alternative diagnosis
Fundoscopy to assess for diabetic retinopathy
Blood pressure assessment and cardiovascular risk evaluation
Renal ultrasound to assess kidney size and exclude obstruction
Consideration of biopsy when the clinical picture is atypical for diabetic disease
redFlags: Rapid decline in renal function suggesting a superimposed or alternative process
Nephrotic-range proteinuria with hypoalbuminaemia and oedema
Active urinary sediment or haematuria pointing to glomerulonephritis
Refractory hypertension or hyperkalaemia complicating renin-angiotensin blockade
reference.prognosis: Without intervention, diabetic kidney disease tends to progress steadily to end-stage kidney disease, and it markedly increases cardiovascular mortality. Intensive control of glycaemia and blood pressure, renin-angiotensin blockade, reduction of albuminuria, and modern kidney-protective therapies can substantially slow decline and reduce cardiovascular events, so early detection and comprehensive risk-factor management materially improve outcomes.
pitfalls: Assuming all kidney disease in a diabetic patient is diabetic nephropathy and missing a treatable alternative
Neglecting albuminuria screening so that intervention starts only after significant function is lost
Failing to intensify renin-angiotensin blockade and other kidney-protective therapy in albuminuric patients
Overlooking the high cardiovascular risk that accompanies diabetic kidney disease
